name: Adenosine deaminase hyperactivity (hereditary haemolytic anaemia)
aliases: hereditary nonspherocytic haemolytic anaemia due to ADA excess

clinicalPearls: An unusual disorder in which increased rather than deficient enzyme activity causes chronic non-spherocytic, Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia
Overactivity of adenosine deaminase depletes the red cell of adenine nucleotides, distinguishing it from the deficiency states
Inheritance is autosomal dominant, so an affected parent and multiple affected generations are typically seen, unlike the recessive enzymopathies
The overexpression reflects a regulatory rather than structural gene abnormality, with enzyme activity markedly raised on assay
Red-cell ATP is characteristically low because the substrate for adenine nucleotide synthesis is diverted and degraded
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating greatly increased red-cell adenosine deaminase activity with reduced ATP, alongside the family history
Management is supportive with folate and transfusion where required; the anaemia is usually mild to moderate
reference.pathophysiology: Adenosine deaminase irreversibly deaminates adenosine to inosine, diverting it away from the salvage pathway that maintains the adenine nucleotide pool. In this disorder the enzyme is markedly overexpressed, so adenosine is degraded excessively and the red cell cannot sustain adequate ATP. The resulting energy deficit compromises the cell's ability to maintain ion gradients and membrane function, shortening survival and producing a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia; unusually, the mechanism is enzyme excess rather than deficiency and the trait is dominantly inherited.
additionalInvestigations: Red-cell adenosine deaminase activity assay demonstrating raised activity
Full blood count, reticulocyte count and blood film
Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Direct antiglobulin test to exclude immune haemolysis
Family studies given the dominant inheritance
redFlags: Severe neonatal jaundice requiring exchange transfusion
Aplastic crisis following parvovirus B19 infection
Transfusional iron overload with long-term support
reference.prognosis: The anaemia is generally mild to moderate and lifelong, and most patients have a good prognosis, though severity can vary within affected families.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis by testing only for enzyme deficiencies and not for overactivity
Missing the dominant inheritance pattern and its implications for family screening
Assuming a membrane disorder when spherocytes are absent
Neglecting iron-overload monitoring in transfused patients
management: Recognise that no therapy corrects the underlying enzyme overactivity, so management is supportive
Supplement folic acid to meet the demands of chronic haemolysis
Provide red-cell transfusion support during symptomatic or severe anaemia
Monitor for and treat transfusional iron overload with chelation when required
Ensure routine vaccination and manage intercurrent illness that may worsen the anaemia
Monitor with full blood count, reticulocytes and haemolysis markers to track severity
Offer genetic counselling and family studies given the autosomal dominant inheritance
